extracted.intended_audience: professional scientists and engineers (astronomy, astrophysics, materials science/corrosion)
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed-content Nature journal issue containing a review/communication on dark nebulae, a review-essay on corrosion of ferrous metals, obituaries and current-events items — aimed at professional scientists and engineers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine dust as the primary obscuring agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various forms in which matter may be distributed in space, by far the most efficient in producing obscuration is fine dust, since this has the greatest superficial area per unit of mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dust particles a few millionths of an inch in diameter will produce most obscuration unless such particles form a negligible proportion by weight of the obscuring cloud. Observational examples include dark markings catalogued by Barnard; some dark regions merge into faintly luminous nebulosity near stars, indicating spatial proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction formula and q‑factor dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: In a cloud composed of spherical particles of radius a and density p, distributed at random with mean density d, the extinction of a beam of light per unit distance will be e stellar magnitudes, where e = 0·814 q a p r (text formula as given). The factor q accounts for complications when particle size is comparable with wavelengths of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For particles more than two or three wavelengths in diameter q ≈ 1. For smaller particles q increases to a maximum (circumference ≈ 1·12 × wavelength) and then diminishes; for very small particles the absorption tends toward A^-4 behaviour (Rayleigh-like). Use of q is essential when predicting selective vs. non‑selective extinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimum particle size for maximum opacity (visual light)
rubrics_metrics.description: For visual light the maximum opacity occurs when the radius is 0·086 μ (0·086 micron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cloud of particles of this size and rock density will exert an absorption of one magnitude if it contains only 1/86 of a milligram of matter per square centimeter of cross-section, regardless of thickness. If particles are smaller (half this size or less), selective absorption increases and can be enormously larger relative to gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiation pressure selectively removes fine particles depending on stellar class
rubrics_metrics.description: Radiation pressure from stars acts strongly on the finest dust: for a particle of the optimum size and water density, the repulsive force of the sun’s radiation is about ten times the gravitational attraction; this pressure varies with stellar spectral type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stars of same brightness, radiation pressure is ~2/3 as great for Class M, increases for whiter stars, and for Class B may be ten times that for solar stars. Dwarf stars scarcely repel dust; giant and luminous Class B stars repel fine dust strongly. This selective removal can explain the limited brightening of luminous portions of dark nebulae near bright stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finest dust cannot be in true equilibrium and will slowly escape
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest dust must continue to be repelled by the stars whatever their distance; it may congregate where repulsive forces from opposite sides nearly balance, but cannot be in true equilibrium and must ultimately escape to indefinite distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect depletion of the finest grain population over time in regions subject to sustained stellar radiation pressure; only coarser particles remain near very luminous stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud self-gravitation required to maintain sharp outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some force operates to hold dark clouds together, evidenced by often sharp outlines; this is probably the gravitational attraction of the cloud itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple spherical-cloud estimates link mass (M, in solar masses) and radius (R, parsecs) to escape velocity (given in text). Observed internal velocities (e.g., Orion luminous gas ~5 km/s variations) set constraints on the mass required to prevent dispersal; numerical estimates imply very large aggregate masses (sufficient to form hundreds of stars) and significant dust fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dust clouds impervious to light are also collisional to particles/electrons
rubrics_metrics.description: Any dust cloud which is impervious to light must also be impervious to particles such as those of which it is composed (and to free-moving electrons) in the sense that such a particle could not traverse the cloud without a practical certainty of collision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collisions inside the cloud may account for the presence or production of dust within the cloud even if dust was not originally primordial. This has implications for cloud evolution and internal processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two mechanisms for transition from dark to luminous nebulosity
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from dark nebulae to luminous nebulosity near stars occurs in two ways: (1) simple reflection of starlight, and (2) excitation of gaseous emission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection nebulosity examples: Pleiades, p Ophiuchi. Gaseous emission example: Orion nebula adjacent to obscuration regions. Distinguishing these mechanisms observationally (spectra, presence/absence of nebular emission lines) is diagnostic of the underlying process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaseous nebular luminosity likely from atomic excitation by high‑temperature stars
rubrics_metrics.description: Both theoretical considerations and observations indicate that the luminosity of gaseous nebulae is probably due to excitation of individual atoms by radiations (aethereal or corpuscular) emanating from neighbouring stars of very high temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Orion, the Trapezium stars are the likely excitation source. The luminous gas is selectively sensitive to incident excitation and need not represent the bulk of the matter present; it is analogous to selective gas emission in cometary comae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nebular appearance varies on astronomical timescales due to internal motions
rubrics_metrics.description: If turbulent motions in the nebula are of similar magnitude in all coordinates, they correspond to proper motions that can alter small-scale nebular detail substantially over a million years (e.g., a wisp may move ~2° in 10^6 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that the current detailed aspect of nebulae (wisps, small structures) evolves over geologically short astronomical times; however the bulk nebula can persist while its small-scale morphology changes as clouds drift into/out of excitation fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of liquid water (plus air) is essential for iron corrosion
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to air, the presence of liquid water is essential to corrosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature strongly accelerates corrosion: rate of oxidation of iron immersed in water at 80°C is more than seven times that at 0°C. Practical implication: parts of ships and plant where water and heat persist (boiler-room tanks, bunkers) are high-risk zones requiring special corrosion-control measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localized conditions (moisture, heat, abrasion, deposits) determine corrosion severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual moisture, unequal waste heat distribution, condensation under sidelights, accumulation of coal and mud in bunkers, and abrasive action exacerbate corrosion; often inside surfaces of tanks/shells are more corroded than outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design, cleaning schedules, and attention to vulnerable spots (e.g., under sidelights, pocket bunkers above boilers) are crucial; assume internal surfaces may need more protection and maintenance than exterior ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt (sea‑spray) deposits accelerate external corrosion above waterline
rubrics_metrics.description: External corrosion of shell plating near the wind and water line is aggravated by alternating wet/dry exposure and by sodium chloride deposits from evaporated sea spray, whose hygroscopic and chemical activity induce corrosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greatest external pitting at the wind/water line; protective strategies (coatings, frequent cleaning) should focus here, and account for motion-induced stimulation of corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective coatings must remain intact; broken coatings can cause severe pitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes like Bower‑Barff (coating with magnetic oxide) provide excellent protection while unbroken, but if the coat cracks or chips the exposed metal is rapidly attacked because the oxide becomes cathode and metal the anode, leading to deep pitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on coatings that can flake without appropriate inspection/maintenance. Mill scale cannot be relied upon as a protection — it should be removed by pickling, weathering, or other methods prior to painting to prevent hidden pitting where scale is later removed or damaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alloying (stainless steel) offers durable protection at higher initial cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Alloying iron with chromium (12–14%) produces 'stainless steel' which is remarkably resistant to neutral corrosion though acids will attack it; the cost is high but may be economically justifiable against recurring painting/maintenance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare lifecycle costs: if painting/maintenance costs (example: average paint cost ~5s per ton, annualised ~1s per ton) are significant, a higher upfront alloy cost may be justified to avoid periodic treatment. Evaluate environment (presence of acids) before specifying stainless variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deoxygenation of water as a corrosion control method — combined mechanical/chemical approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal of dissolved oxygen from waters in contact with metal can reduce corrosion; mechanical deaerators can remove much oxygen but are limited by gas solubility, temperature, and achievable vacuum; chemical methods can remove residual oxygen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical plants combine mechanical deaeration (bulk removal) with chemical treatment for the last 5–10% of dissolved oxygen. Operational details matter: e.g., 'deactivator' tanks filled with steel lathing will rust and deoxygenate water but must be correctly charged (avoid compacted turnings that block flow); filters may be needed to remove suspended iron hydroxide. Examples: Balke mechanical deaerator (spray in vacuum chamber) and Pittsburgh plant (1915) with deactivator plus filter).
